Senses.Explanation: A comic epithet for a one-sided person: a fellow carrying a board and seeing only one side. The stock line says that Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side, while Baiyu Jingsi states directly that each party sees one side and is precisely a board-carrying fellow (各見一邊，正是擔板漢). In a case Baiyu raises, Muezhou Daozong calls to an addressee and applies the name when the man turns; Xuedou Chongxian and Huanglong Huinan then debate its application, and Baiyu judges their opposed comments one-sided. The label extends beyond that case. Dongshan Meixi Du says that learning without awakening is overbearing pride, whereas awakening without learning is a board-carrying fellow (有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢). Zhe'an Jingfan applies it both to delight at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket, and elsewhere says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients only makes such a fellow before asking how the matter can be raised whole (只成擔板漢，此事如何舉得全). Yuanwu Keqin says that a board-carrying fellow often dies in the phrase (若是擔板漢，多向句中死却). Zen bends a comic physical image into a public epithet for the person whom a record presents as fixed on one side or trapped in wording; the entry reports those attested applications without generalizing beyond them.

Senses.Explanation: To assume and bear responsibility, especially for the teaching or its succession. Yuanwu Keqin places successful shouldering beside accepting, heading toward, and carrying out; elsewhere he says only Shenguang was permitted to bear the subtle key of Shaolin. Guangzhi Quanwu calls for someone able to shoulder it with the whole body, and Xueqiao Yuanxin calls a person with strength to come forward and bear it on one shoulder. Jiufeng Daoqian explicitly defines inward accepting and shouldering as inner succession, then contrasts it with the person who has no accepting and no shouldering. These responsibility, authority, and succession frames make the omitted load institutional and figurative. They are a different referent from physically carrying cargo, even though the metaphor retains the bodily image.

SearchAliases: carry snow to fill a well
Senses.Explanation: Carrying snow to fill a well is a recurrent comparison for ineffective effort, applied to talk, question-and-answer, sitting Chan, and other undertakings. Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" : the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" , to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" , and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" . Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball . Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

Senses.Explanation: The fixed appraisal ‘the substance stands exposed’ occurs in ‘true constancy stands exposed,’ ‘the whole substance stands exposed,’ and the recurrent ‘the substance stands exposed in the golden wind’ case; the grammar leaves ‘body’ versus ‘substance’ open where the record does. Literally, “body or substance” and “exposed”: “body or substance exposed.” The compound occurs 646 times in 222 allowlisted texts. Its syntax varies: the body or constant substance is exposed, while the preceding word “whole” can make the entire body exposed. One discourse explicitly says that when feelings about holy and ordinary are exhausted, this is called “true constancy, body exposed.” Another recurrent statement says, “True constancy, body exposed, not constrained by written words.” The fixed Yunmen exchange asks, “What about when the tree withers and the leaves fall?” and answers, “Body exposed in the autumn wind.” That four-graph answer occurs 176 times in 100 texts and is repeatedly raised, versified, and questioned by later masters. Other expansions include “body exposed, imposing and evident” and “the whole body exposed.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 門云：體露金風
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1435.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai (無異元來禪師廣錄): Complete source unit: Yunmen Wenyan is the quoted utterer of the body exposed in the golden wind; Wuyi Yuanlai is the later local raiser or commentator, not the utterer of the quoted answer.

Senses.Explanation: The body exposed in the golden wind is Yunmen Wenyan's compact answer to the public question, 'When the trees are bare and the leaves have fallen, what then?' Later masters repeatedly raise, criticize, and answer the case, while verse authors carry its autumn scene into frost, leaves, river, moon and wind. 'Golden wind' is thus the autumn wind in the phrase's observable scene; the Chan pressure lies in presenting total exposure as the immediate answer, without supplying an object hidden behind it.
